description: ¡Hola! Soy Juan, ingeniero backend de Medellín (Java, Spring WebFlux, IA aplicada). Construimos "Vesta Zero", un dashboard con IA que resume y explica décadas de datos de combustión en microgravedad de la NASA para seguridad contra incendios en misiones a la Luna y Marte. Backend e IA cubiertos. Busco: frontend/visualización de datos, diseño UI/UX, perfil científico o de ingeniería o quien tenga ganas de crear ciencia. Todos los niveles son bienvenidos. ¡Únete!
summary:
Vesta Zero is an AI-assisted web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into fire safety insights for crewed exploration. It loads the 24 fire-related investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, including their experimental tables (1,969 documented tests), and lets users rank, compare and query them.

It addresses the challenge in four ways. It ranks investigations by relevance to a chosen crew environment (spacecraft cabin, lunar base and pressurized rover, Martian base, spacesuit) with a transparent, adjustable score. It summarizes each investigation with AI: fuels and samples, sensors, what changed and what stayed constant between tests, and Earth applications, each item traced to the verbatim PSI passage. It answers questions with an assistant that cites every investigation by DOI and never invents numbers. It exports test conditions (oxygen, pressure, flow) as CSV or JSON for flammability modeling.

This matters because lunar habitats and rovers are expected to run at 30 % oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, which makes materials far more flammable than on Earth. Vesta Zero puts the relevant evidence in one place for students, researchers and engineers, and it shows the gaps clearly: PSI has no partial-gravity data yet.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Vesta Zero is a dashboard for students, educators, researchers and aerospace engineers who need fire safety evidence for crewed spacecraft and habitats. It has five views:

1. Catalog: the 24 fire-related PSI investigations (ACME, CFI, FLEX, FLEX-2, BASS, BASS-II, SPICE, SLICE, SAFFIRE-I/II/III, SAME, SAME-R, DAFT, and five ground studies that model flight data), with filters by safety pillar (prevention, detection, suppression), hardware and fuel type.

2. Investigation detail: objectives, approach, hardware, DOI, the documented test conditions from the experimental tables, and an AI summary (fuels and samples, sensors and measurements, test variables, test constants, Earth applications). Every AI item opens the exact PSI passage it comes from.

3. Ranking: pick a crew environment and get an explainable score. Five weighted criteria: closeness of the tested atmosphere to the target, relevance to crew environments, material type, safety pillar, and availability of structured data. Users can move the weights, and each result shows its breakdown per criterion.

4. Compare: two or three investigations side by side, with computed similarities and differences and an optional AI comparison.

5. Assistant: natural-language questions answered only from the loaded records, with a citation (PSI ID and DOI) for every claim.

A Data page filters the documented test conditions across investigations (for example, the lunar habitat range of at least 30 % O2 at 10.2 psi or less returns 74 tests) and downloads them as CSV or JSON, with the DOI to cite on every row.

HOW IT WORKS

- Ingestion: a backend job reads the PSI metadata and the experimental-table CSVs (22 files from 20 investigations), with one request every 2 seconds and no raw data downloads. Tables use mixed formats (oxygen as fraction or percent, pressure in atm, bar or mmHg, units inside cells), so each file has a curated column mapping and validation limits. Values that cannot be normalized are never guessed: they are logged as warnings and the original row is kept.

- Ranking: deterministic and explainable. It does not use AI, so the same inputs always give the same result.

- AI extraction: Claude reads each investigation once, offline, and returns structured JSON. A verifier keeps an item only if its source passage is found in the PSI record and every number in the item appears in that passage. Results are stored with the model and prompt version.

- Assistant: all 24 records fit in one prompt. Answers are structured JSON; citations and numbers are checked against the records, and anything that does not match is shown as a warning. Answers are cached, so a repeated question makes no new API call.

- Provenance: every value is labeled "Documented" (from PSI) or "AI-extracted".

- Scope notices: the dashboard shows that PSI has no partial-gravity data yet (expected from LUCI and FM2), that E-FIELD only mimics partial gravity with electric fields, and that rockets and propellants are out of PSI's scope. Martian base targets are marked as an assumption.

BENEFITS

- Engineers and researchers find the most relevant microgravity fire evidence for a specific habitat atmosphere in seconds, and see why it ranks where it does.

- Students and educators get plain-language summaries that stay tied to the original source and DOI.

- Modelers get a clean, citable table of tested oxygen, pressure and flow conditions across investigations.

- Earth applications (smoke detectors, water-mist suppression, firefighter equipment) are surfaced from the same records.

WHAT I HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A trustworthy entry point to NASA's combustion data for the next generation of lunar and Martian habitat designers, ready to add LUCI and FM2 partial-gravity results when they are published.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 3.5, Spring WebFlux (functional routes), R2DBC, PostgreSQL 16, Flyway, Gradle. Hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture, with dependency rules enforced by ArchUnit tests.

- Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4.

- AI: Claude (Anthropic) through the Anthropic Java SDK, called from the backend only.

- Infrastructure: Docker Compose. The repository includes a database seed, so the dashboard runs locally with one command and no API key.
